samples.summary: Image downloads now force a per-request undici `Agent`, silently bypassing any globally configured dispatcher (HTTP/HTTPS proxy)
samples.evidence: `createImageFetcher` builds `pinnedAgent(addresses)` and passes it as `dispatcher` on every hop (`{ redirect: 'manual', ...(agent ? { dispatcher: agent } : {}) }`). An explicit dispatcher overrides undici's global dispatcher, so a proxy installed via `setGlobalDispatcher(new ProxyAgent(...))` or Node's `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY` handling is ignored: the connector dials the resolved IPs directly. Worse, on a machine that can only reach the internet through a proxy the gate's own `defaultLookup` (`dns.lookup`) and the direct connect will both fail, so `docs/slides export` of any document containing an external image now fails with `NETWORK_ERROR` where it previously succeeded through the proxy. Nothing in the change restores the ambient dispatcher's proxy settings on the pinned agent.

samples.summary: `isOpaqueRedirect` conflates a genuine network-error Response (`status === 0`, type `'error'`) with an opaque redirect, causing a real outbound request that bypasses the injected transport
samples.evidence: `return res.type === 'opaqueredirect' || res.status === 0;`. `Response.error()` — the sentinel a fetch implementation returns for a *network failure* — has `type === 'error'` and `status === 0`. When the caller-supplied `fetch` seam returns one (or any 0-status response), the code falls into `rawRequest(target, agent)`, which calls `undiciRequest` directly and therefore ignores `fetchImpl` entirely and issues a real network request. `packages/cli/test/image-fetcher.test.ts:507` relies on exactly this, so the seam documented on `ImageFetcherOptions.fetch` ("a seam for tests") is not actually authoritative: a stub that reports a transport failure gets silently retried against the live network.

samples.summary: `rawRequest` constructs `new Response(body, { status })` which throws for null-body statuses (204/205/304) and for informational statuses
samples.evidence: `return new Response(Readable.toWeb(res.body) as ReadableStream<Uint8Array>, { status: res.statusCode, headers });` — the WHATWG `Response` constructor throws `TypeError: Response with null body status cannot have body` for 204/205/304 and `RangeError` for a status below 200. `res.body` from `undiciRequest` is always a stream, never `null`, so any such upstream status reaching this fallback raises an unclassified throw that escapes the `try` in `rawRequest` (which only wraps the `undiciRequest` call), producing a stack trace instead of the CLI's error envelope/exit classification.

samples.summary: A malformed `Location` header raises a raw `TypeError` that escapes the change's own classification scheme
samples.evidence: `target = new URL(location, target).toString();` is not guarded. A redirect whose `Location` is unparseable relative to `target` (e.g. `Location: ://x`) throws a bare `TypeError`, which `exitCodeFor` maps to the user-error class with a message like `Invalid URL` — i.e. a misbehaving remote server is reported as the caller's mistake, defeating the exit contract this PR is built around. Every other failure on this path is deliberately wrapped (`blocked`, `httpError`, `fetchOrThrow`); this one is not.

samples.summary: Redirect-limit path leaks the last hop's response body (not cancelled before throwing)
samples.evidence: In the `hop >= MAX_REDIRECTS` branch the code throws `blocked(...)` *before* the `await res.body?.cancel()` two lines below, so the final response body is never drained/cancelled. The `finally` only calls `agent.destroy()`, which is fire-and-forget (`void ... .catch(() => {})`) and races the un-cancelled stream. Every other exit from the loop cancels the body first — this one is the exception.

samples.summary: `mayBeServer` is a port-only test, so the server-address exemption is consulted for every same-port image URL and grants any host sharing an IP with the API server
samples.evidence: `const mayBeServer = server !== null && effectivePort(url) === effectivePort(server);` — for the default production server (`https://…`, port 443) this is true for *every* https image URL. Two consequences: (1) an extra DNS resolution of the server host is performed per image (`serverAddresses`), doubling lookups on the hot path; (2) the per-address exemption `exempt.has(a.toLowerCase())` then allows *any* host that resolves to one of the API server's addresses — common on shared CDN/edge IPs — skipping the private-address check for it. The comment claims only "a port match is worth resolving a name for", but with a default port that is effectively every URL.

samples.summary: `process.exit(exitCode)` immediately after `console.error` can truncate the login failure message when stderr is a pipe
`callbackPromise` is created eagerly and can reject before any handler is attached, producing an unhandled rejection
samples.evidence: `const callbackPromise = new Promise<string>((res, rej) => {...})` is created inside `startCallbackServer`, and the timeout at line 410 rejects it unconditionally when `!settled`. In `runLogin` the promise is only observed at line 217 (`await waitForCallback()`), after `await import('open')` and `await open(oauthUrl)`. If those stall past `timeoutMs` (a hung browser launcher, or a test/caller that passes a small `timeoutMs` and does not immediately await), the rejection is unobserved and Node terminates the process on `unhandledRejection` rather than reporting the classified login error. `close()` also never rejects the promise, so a caller that closes without awaiting leaves it pending forever.

samples.summary: Rerouting API-key calls through `sendJson` produces a `SESSION_EXPIRED` body that the command then discards in favour of a generic auth message
samples.evidence: `HttpClient.sendJson` now returns `{ ok: false, status: 401, data: { error: { code: 'SESSION_EXPIRED', ... } } }` when the refresh fails (`http-client.ts:190-192`), but `api-keys.ts` does `if (!res.ok) throw httpError(res.status);` for all three commands, which discards `res.data` and emits `AUTH_ERROR` / "Authentication failed. Run `wafflebase login`." The more specific machine-readable `SESSION_EXPIRED` code the refactor just started producing never reaches stderr, unlike the docs/notes/slides commands which print `res.data` verbatim.

samples.summary: `runFilesDownload` maps a successful-but-bodyless response to `exitCodeForStatus(200)`, i.e. reports a user error for a server-side anomaly
samples.evidence: `if (!res.ok || !res.bytes) { ... return { exitCode: exitCodeForStatus(res.status) }; }` — the `!res.bytes` disjunct is reachable with `res.ok === true` and `res.status === 200`, in which case `exitCodeForStatus(200)` returns `EXIT_USER_ERROR` (1) even though the failure is "the server sent no bytes", exactly the system-fault class this PR introduces exit 2 for. The new comment ("The status decides the exit class") only reasons about the `!res.ok` case.

samples.summary: Under a spec-conformant `redirect: 'manual'` every redirect hop is requested twice
samples.evidence: The WHATWG spec mandates that `redirect: 'manual'` yield an opaque-redirect filtered response (status 0, no headers) — the code's own `isOpaqueRedirect` doc block acknowledges this. If undici implements the filter (it follows the spec closely in the fetch path), then for each redirect hop `fetchOrThrow` issues request #1, gets the filtered shell, and `rawRequest` immediately re-issues the *same* request #2 to read status + `Location`. The comment asserts "undici … hands back the real response instead", which if wrong makes the double-request the normal path rather than a rare fallback; the real-listener test passes either way, so nothing pins which behaviour is in effect.

finding.summary: Image downloads now force a per-request undici `Agent`, silently bypassing any globally configured dispatcher (HTTP/HTTPS proxy)
finding.evidence: `createImageFetcher` builds `pinnedAgent(addresses)` and passes it as `dispatcher` on every hop (`{ redirect: 'manual', ...(agent ? { dispatcher: agent } : {}) }`). An explicit dispatcher overrides undici's global dispatcher, so a proxy installed via `setGlobalDispatcher(new ProxyAgent(...))` or Node's `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY` handling is ignored: the connector dials the resolved IPs directly. Worse, on a machine that can only reach the internet through a proxy the gate's own `defaultLookup` (`dns.lookup`) and the direct connect will both fail, so `docs/slides export` of any document containing an external image now fails with `NETWORK_ERROR` where it previously succeeded through the proxy. Nothing in the change restores the ambient dispatcher's proxy settings on the pinned agent.

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as quoted. `pinnedAgent` (image-fetcher.ts:341-363) builds a fresh undici `Agent` with a connector-level `lookup` restricted to the gate-approved IPs, and it is attached as `dispatcher` on every hop of the redirect loop (image-fetcher.ts:467, 471-476) and on the raw-request fallback (image-fetcher.ts:393-396), against the userland undici `fetch` (image-fetcher.ts:426; undici is a direct dep, packages/cli/package.json:30). An explicit `dispatcher` in the init takes precedence over any globally installed dispatcher, and I found no code anywhere in the repo (grep for ProxyAgent/HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY/NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY/setGlobalDispatcher outside node_modules returned zero matches) that carries proxy settings onto the pinned agent or otherwise makes this path unreachable, so `already-guarded` does not apply and `not-present` is false. The described failure surface is also real: `defaultLookup` is `dns.lookup` (image-fetcher.ts:428-429) and `resolveHost` maps failures to `SystemError('NETWORK_ERROR', ...)` (image-fetcher.ts:208-233), and on a host where DNS resolves but direct egress is blocked the gate passes at line 310 while only the pinned direct connect fails — i.e. the dispatcher is the deciding factor and an export of any document with an external image fails. I considered `out-of-scope` because address pinning is inherently incompatible with a forward proxy and is a security-hardening tradeoff, but the finding is framed as a functional break of a core flow (docs/slides export), which is squarely correctness impact, so I cannot drop it under this rubric.
